If I could do one thing to help Oklahoma make better decisions about complex, long-term weather-related problems, it would be to create a statewide, nonpartisan climate and infrastructure council with real authority, not just advisory power. Too often, decisions about water use, drought planning, severe storms, and extreme heat are made in short political cycles, while the problems themselves unfold over decades. This mismatch leads to reactive policies instead of proactive ones.

This council would bring together scientists, local leaders, farmers, energy experts, and urban planners to translate data into clear, actionable policy. Just as important, it would be required to communicate risks to the public in plain language, so voters understand the stakes behind decisions on things like flood control, grid resilience, and land use. When people grasp the long-term costs of inaction—whether it’s worsening tornado damage or water scarcity—they’re more likely to support smart investments.

Finally, the council would tie funding to evidence-based planning, ensuring that state resources go toward projects proven to reduce risk over time. Oklahoma doesn’t lack knowledge; it struggles with consistency and follow-through. A permanent, accountable body focused on long-term outcomes would help bridge that gap and lead to more resilient, forward-thinking decisions.
